newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil sugar sector hopes to be freed by year-end.
newsitem.headline: Brazil sugar sector hopes to be freed by year-end.

text.p: Brazil's government could announce as early as next month a zero tax on exports of sugar not included in its 1997/98 crop plan, effectively liberalizing the domestic sugar sector, industry officials said.
A working group of government officials is currently looking at mechanisms to liberate additional exports from tariffs.

"A working commission was created, it has until July 9 to present its conclusion," Sergio Simoes Ometto, president of the Sao Paulo Sugar Industry Union (Unica), told Reuters at a seminar on the future of alcohol production. "We think it's possible (they will announce the liberalization of the sector)," he added.

Under the 1997/98 crop plan, the Brazilian government has allocated 5.39 million tonnes of sugar for export out of a total estimated production of 13.48 million tonnes, only marginally up on last year's export quota of 5.2 million tonnes.

It controls the flow of exports with an export tax, last year of up to 40 percent, which applies to sugars in excess of the export quota. The government has pledged to liberalize the sugar and hydrous alcohol sectors by May 1998.

"This group must liberalize sugar exports before the end of this harvest," said Aloisio Almeida, head of economics and institutional relations at Copersucar, which accounts for a quarter of Brazil's sugar and alcohol market.
"We think this process is inexorable and that it must occur during this harvest," he said, adding that exports should rise between five and 10 percent as a result.

Other industry officials said it was not the volume of exports that mattered so much so each company should be free to export as much as they could without having to buy up quotas from other producers.

"The important thing is not the volume. Economically the moment is right for liberalization and the important thing is that I am able to export at the right moment (for me)," said Luis Carlos Correa Carvalho, a consultant at Unica.

The working commission, created in May, is scheduled to hold another meeting before the end of the month but no date has yet been set, said Pedro Cabral, head of the sugar and alcohol sector at the Ministry of Industry and Commerce. "We will respect all deadlines," he said.
Sugar producers said they were anxious to see which steps the group announces in conjunction with liberalizing exports. In particular, they want measures to support the domestic alcohol sector.

"The forecasts for hydrous alcohol production contained in this crop plan are excessive and they will have to be adjusted," said Copersucar's Almeida. "Brazil does not need to import another drop of alcohol."

The industry was urgently demanding measures to eliminate the current use of alcohol substituting fuels such as a mixture of methanol, gasoline and alcohol, Almeida said. But most importantly, it wants the sugar sector to receive the same treatment as other Brazilian export markets, such as soybeans.
"With the availability of sugar cane we have this harvest, we don't see any reason for the sugar sector to be treated differently from any other sector of the market," Almeida said.
